name: Oil Impasto
basis: why: thick paint stands up and is read as light on relief; how: stroke colour and height maps, bristle furrows, lit

lumenary.blurb: Thick oil paint laid on with a loaded brush: ridged strokes that catch the light from one side.

facts.bestOn: Landscapes and portraits with strong light

why: Thick oil paint stands up from the canvas, and most of what we read as paint is light and shadow on that relief. So this treatment builds two pictures from the same brush strokes: a colour map and a height map. Each stroke is a small ridged landscape with bristle furrows and piled-up lips, and one light does the rest.
how: Scatter short fat strokes over a jittered grid, with a second pass at half the size for details.
Give each stroke the colour of the blurred picture at its centre, varied by 6 percent, and an angle that mixes the picture’s edge direction with a loose random direction.
In the height map, make each stroke a base height with three thin bristle furrows and bright lips on both sides where paint piles up.
Blur the map slightly and take its slopes by finite differences, scaled by the thickness slider.
Light the result with a diffuse term for broad shading and a highlight for the wet shine.
history: Oil paint became the main medium of European painting in the fifteenth century, and Rembrandt used thick paint to make highlights rise from a flat ground. Impasto was pushed much further by Vincent van Gogh in the 1880s. The collapsible metal paint tube, patented by John Goffe Rand in 1841, let painters carry colours outdoors.
uses: Fine art style prints and posters
terms: Paint applied so thickly that brush strokes stand out.
Estimating a slope by subtracting nearby values.
A thin groove left by one hair of the brush.
paragraphs: Thick oil paint stands up from the canvas, and most of what we read as paint is light and shadow on that relief. So two pictures are made with the same brush strokes: a colour map and a height map. Short fat strokes are scattered over a jittered grid (spacing about 0.95 of the brush size), with a second pass at half the size covering a third of the grid for the details. Each stroke takes the colour of the blurred picture at its centre, varied by ±6%, and lies at an angle that mixes two directions: along the picture’s edges (the gradient direction turned by 90 degrees) and a loose random direction near −40 degrees. The mix weight is the follow-the-shapes slider times the local edge strength.

In the height map each stroke is a little ridged landscape: a base height, three thin parallel bristle furrows along its length, and bright lips at both sides where paint piles up. The map is blurred slightly and its slopes are taken by finite differences, scaled by the thickness slider. From the slopes comes a surface normal, and the light does the rest: a diffuse term for the broad shading and a Blinn-Phong highlight for the wet shine, with the light direction set by the angle slider.

equations.note: Stroke angle: φ is the gradient direction, θ₀ the loose random direction, f the follow-the-shapes slider.
s_x and s_y are the slopes of the height map, magnified by 1 to 9 with the thickness slider.
Diffuse shading plus a specular glint. l is the unit light direction (l_z = 0.7 before normalising), h its half-vector with the viewer, σ the wet shine slider.

presets.text: A large brush with thick paint is bold and sculptural.
A small brush that follows shapes closely keeps detail.
Move the light to the top to change every shadow.
